messages.content: Calculate the standard deviation of the null hypothesis test with a sample mean of 98.2, standard deviation of 1.4, and sample size of 40 for a population mean of 98.6.

function.name: statistics_calculate_p_value
function.description: Calculate the p-value for a t-test on a single sample from a population. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

sample_mean.description: The mean of the sample data. This is a float type value.

population_mean.description: The mean of the population data. This is a float type value.

sample_std_dev.description: The standard deviation of the sample data. This is a float type value.

sample_size.description: The size of the sample data.

two_tailed.description: Whether the test is two-tailed. If not provided, default is true.

message.reasoning:
The user says "Calculate the standard deviation of the null hypothesis test" but they provide sample mean, standard deviation, sample size, and population mean. They likely want the standard error or the t-statistic? They say "standard deviation of the null hypothesis test". That might refer to the standard error of the sampling distribution under H0: sqrt(s^2/n). But they gave sample std dev 1.4. So standard error = 1.4 / sqrt(40) ≈ 1.4/6.3249=0.2215. Or maybe they want the standard deviation of the sampling distribution of the mean under H0: sigma/sqrt(n). But we don't know population sigma; we use sample sigma as estimate. So answer: ~0.2215.

But they also mention "for a population mean of 98.6". That might be used to compute t-statistic: (98.2-98.6)/(1.4/sqrt(40)) = -0.4/0.2215 = -1.805. But question: "Calculate the standard deviation of the null hypothesis test". Might be standard error. So answer: 0.2215.

We can also compute p-value using the function. Let's do that. Use two-tailed test. Compute t-statistic: t = (98.2-98.6)/0.2215 = -1.805. Degrees of freedom df=39. Compute p-value. Use python.
